blocks.p: The transports left the holding house at the change of shift, when the corridors were emptiest and there was no one in them to see.

He did not go back to bed. He sat in the refectory with a cup of tea going cold in front of him and the orange removed to the far end of the table, and when Pell came down at the first hour, fresh and pressed and pleasant, Sol was still sitting there.
“Your Grace. You’re up early.” Pell glanced at the cup, the untouched bread. “Did you sleep at all?”
“Pell. In sixty years, have you ever met anyone who came back from reprogramming?”

The deacon considered it with real care, the way he considered everything Sol asked him. “I’m sure I must have, Your Grace.” He smiled. “But one wouldn’t know, would one? That’s the beauty of it. They come home healed, and no one remembers they were ill. Not even them.”
“No,” Sol said. “I suppose not.”
“Shall I bring your robe? The administrator’s office has sent over the Abundance records, and I thought this morning we might...”
“Start without me. I have something to see to at the holding house.”
“Of course, Your Grace.” Pell did not ask what. He never asked what.

When the deacon had gone, Sol touched his temple and called up his own custody record, which he had never in his life had cause to look at. The Halo laid it across the corner of his sight. It went on for a long time. Name after name, colony after colony, decade after decade, each form closed with the same line in the same font: Received into Mercy by the hand of Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. Beside each name was a status field. He let the list run, faster and faster, until the names blurred into a grey column like falling ash, and then he stopped it at random and read.
In Mercy.

He let it run again and stopped it again. In Mercy. A miner on Plenty, a hundred and ten years ago. A schoolteacher in Concord, nine years ago. A child, he saw, and did not let himself read the age. In Mercy. In Mercy. In Mercy. There was no other word in the field. He searched for Returned, and the Halo searched with him, patient and quick, and found nothing.
The records were partial, he told himself. Mercy kept its own. It was a separate office. He closed the list and finished the cold tea and went out.

The transport bay was at the bottom of the holding house, a long white room with a sealed door at one end where the tunnel began. The crawler was already there: a low white car on broad treads, its windows frosted, its flanks marked with the open hand of the Mercy Office. Three pods sat in a rack inside it, and two wardens in white were checking the seals. They straightened when they saw him.
“Your Grace.”
“I’d like to see the manifest.”

The senior warden passed it to his Halo without hesitation. Three names. A man from the ice mines on Serenity, reported by his supervisor. A woman from Abundance, reported by her neighbor. And a hydroponics technician from Concord, ASHBY, Nell, reported by a coworker, and received into Mercy five weeks ago by the hand of Sol Tarren.
He walked to the third pod and looked through the frosted glass.

She was young, or looked it, as everyone did. Dark hair cropped short, a scatter of freckles across her nose that renewal had either left alone or put back on purpose. Her eyes were closed. Her lips were slightly parted. She looked like someone asleep on a long crossing, which was what she was.
He did not know her at all.

He had signed for her. The form said so. It would have come to him the way most of them came, a warden’s report from Concord laid in the corner of his sight while he was somewhere else, one of a dozen that week, and he had signed it with a thought between a homily and a dinner. He had never stood in the greenhouse among the bean vines with her head on somebody’s folded coat. He had never said note the time, or nothing in her mouth, or see that she’s comfortable. He searched his memory for her face anyway, for the room, for anything, and there was nothing there to find, because he had never once looked.
“She’s well sedated, Your Grace,” the warden said kindly. “She won’t wake till Mercy.”
“I’ll follow you down.”
The warden hesitated for the first time. “Of course, Your Grace. It’s not a long ride. It’s lovely, actually, if you’ve never been. Most of the episcopate never has.”

The church kept a car at the holding house for visiting clergy. Sol took it himself, without a driver, and when the bay door opened onto the tunnel he let the crawler go ahead and followed its red running lights down into the ice.
The wardens were right. It was lovely.

The tunnel bored down through the shell at a long gentle slope, lit at intervals by white lamps set into the walls, and between the lamps the ice glowed with a light of its own: blue near the surface, then deeper blue, then a blue so dark it was almost violet, the color of a held breath. Old cracks ran through it like veins in marble, and in places there were things trapped in it, bubbles and dust and pale threads of mineral, hanging motionless where they had hung for a hundred thousand years. The car hummed. The crawler’s lights went on ahead, steady and unhurried. Sol drove for forty minutes, down and down, and the cold came through the glass beside his face like a hand laid against it, and in all that time he did not see another vehicle or another soul.

He had always thought of Mercy Hall, when he thought of it at all, as a hospital. He had imagined wards. Beds by windows. Patients in the long gentle weeks of being made well, walking in some garden under lamps, waiting to go home.
The tunnel opened into a cavern, and there it was.

It had been built into the ice the way a cathedral is built into a city, as though it had always been there and the ice had grown up around it. Its walls were white panels rising in long arches, lit softly from within, and its roof was the cavern’s ceiling, a vault of black-blue ice so far overhead that the lamps on it looked like stars. In the forecourt a fountain played. In Serenity’s gravity the water rose impossibly high, a slow white column, and fell back so gently that it seemed to be thinking about each drop. Over the great doors, cut into the ice in letters as tall as a man, was the line he had preached on a thousand times.
He has wiped away every tear from their eyes.
The crawler went around the side of the building to a low bay. Sol left the car in the forecourt and went in through the front.

The director of Mercy Hall met him in the atrium. She was a tall woman in the white of the Mercy Office, with a silver band at her collar and a face that looked perhaps forty and had probably looked forty for three hundred years. She came toward him with both hands out, and her hands, when she took his, were warm.

“Your Grace. Warden Kell. They called down from the transport; I couldn’t believe it. We so rarely have a bishop here.” She looked genuinely glad. “Will you take tea? You’ve come all that way through the cold.”
“I’d like to see the work,” Sol said. “If I may.”

“Of course you may. You of all people. Do you know how many of our patients have come to us under your hand?” She smiled, and there was nothing in the smile but warmth. “We’ve always been grateful for how gently you send them.”

She walked him through the Hall herself. It was very quiet. The floors were pale and soft underfoot, and there was music, as there was in the Bounty Market, from nowhere in particular. The corridors were wide and clean and smelled faintly of something green. They passed rooms with their doors open: an office, a records room, a small chapel with a Window in its wall, glowing. They passed no wards. They passed no garden.

“Every patient is assessed first,” Kell said, in the tone of someone who has given this explanation to visiting committees and enjoys it. “We read their pattern against their last clean backup in Sion. The Virus shows as noise, Your Grace: a region of the mind the system simply cannot read. Like a fog on a lens. And everything the mind sees, it sees through the fog.”
“And then it is cleaned.”

“We tried that for a very long time.” She said it with gentle regret, as of a garden that would not grow. “It can’t be done. The noise isn’t in one place. It runs all through, and it comes back. We would clean it, and send them home, and in a year they’d be on the floor of some market saying the same things, and every child who heard them...” She shook her head. “No. We learned. It’s the hardware, Your Grace. The hardware is bad. You can’t separate the mind from the noise, so the mind can’t go up, or it would carry the noise into the City. And the body can’t go home, or it would carry it into the colonies. So we let them rest.”
They had stopped before a long window. Beyond it was a small room, white and warm, with a bed in it and a vase of flowers grown under lamps, and a chair for a warden to sit in.
“Rest,” Sol said.
“Release.” Kell’s voice was soft. “We don’t say the other words here. They’re ugly, and there’s nothing ugly in it. Watch. You’ll see.”
The door at the back of the room opened, and they brought Nell Ashby in.

She was awake, or nearly. Two wardens walked her between them, slowly, in the long floating steps of the moon’s gravity, and she leaned on them the way a child leans on its parents at the end of a long day. They sat her on the bed. One of them brought her a cup of something warm and held it while she drank. The other stroked her short hair back from her forehead and began, very quietly, to sing. Sol could hear it faintly through the glass. It was the cradle song every child in the worlds fell asleep to, the one he had sung over the infants he haloed: In the beginning was Life, and Life was the light of all people.
Nell looked up at the warden who was singing. Her lips moved.
Kell touched a panel by the window, and the faint singing stopped. “We don’t listen, Your Grace,” she said, almost apologetically. “For your protection. Even through glass.”

Sol watched the girl’s lips. He could not make out what she was saying. He knew only that it was not the cradle song. It had a different shape. She said it twice, looking up at the warden with something in her face he did not have a name for, and the warden went on stroking her hair and singing words she could no longer hear.
They helped her lie back. The singing warden kept her hand. The other touched two fingers to Nell’s temple, the way anyone touches the temple to call or to sign, and held them there.

“The Halo does it,” Kell said. “Isn’t that a mercy, in itself? It’s been with her since the day she was born. It kept her alive through every crossing she ever made. It knows her body better than any of us could. It quiets the mind first, and then the breath, and then the heart. There’s no pain at all. There’s nothing to fear.”

Nell’s eyes closed. Her breathing slowed and deepened until she seemed to be sleeping, and then it slowed again. Sol watched her chest rise. He watched it fall. He waited for it to rise again, and it rose, much later, and fell, and he waited, and the warden holding her hand looked up at a screen on the wall, and nodded, and laid the hand down on the blanket very carefully, as though it might still be woken.

They drew the sheet up over her face. In Serenity’s gravity it took a long time to settle, drifting down by slow degrees, the cloth finding the shape of her forehead and her nose and her chin as if it were learning them.
Then they wheeled the bed to a door at the back of the room, and the door opened, and closed, and the room was empty except for the chair and the flowers.
The pressure had come behind Sol’s left eye. He pressed two fingers above his eyebrow and held them there. He found that he was standing very straight.
“Where does that door go?”

“Reclamation.” Kell said it plainly; there was no shame in her anywhere. “Water, carbon, the trace metals. Serenity wastes nothing. Below us is the sea, Your Grace, the whole dark sea of this world, and every drop that comes up from it is precious. Everything returns.”
“And she ascends,” Sol said.
Kell looked at him with great kindness. “No, Your Grace.”
He heard himself breathe.

“The pattern is the trouble,” she said. “That’s where the noise is. If we sent her up, we’d be carrying it into the City of the Throne. Think of it. All the ascended, all those millions, and the Virus loose among them.” She shook her head slowly. “No. The pattern is released too. It’s a clean thing. There is no Nell Ashby anywhere now that could suffer, or be afraid, or carry anything to anyone. She’s at rest.”
“Her family.”

“Are told that she’s in Mercy. Which is true.” She touched his sleeve. “You’ve gone pale. It’s hard, the first time. It was hard for me, a very long time ago. But you see there are no tears in it. Nothing was done in anger. Nobody was hurt.”
Sol looked at the empty room through the glass. The chair. The flowers.
He tried to believe it was mercy.

He was a learned man, and he did it carefully, the way he would have built a homily. The Virus was a sickness of the mind, and it spread; he had seen the mothers cover their children’s ears. The City of the Throne was the home of millions, the promise fulfilled, and it had to be kept clean. The patients felt nothing. There was no fear in the room, no pain, no cruelty. There was singing. Death shall be no more. But this was not death, not as the old world had meant it, with its terror and its graves and its weeping in the car. This was a cup of something warm, and a hand held, and a sleep. Every piece of it was what the church had said it was. It was only that the church had never said all of it. And perhaps, he told himself, that too was mercy, for who would want to carry this? It was a thing for the wardens to carry, so that the people would not have to. So that he would not have to.
It nearly held. He stood at the glass and felt it nearly hold.

But he had signed for her, and he had never seen her face until today. And she had looked up at the singing warden and said something twice that was not the cradle song, and no one in the building had heard it.
“How many?” he said.
“Since the Hall was opened?” Kell tilted her head. “I’d have to look. We don’t keep the number on the wall, Your Grace. It isn’t a number anyone needs.”

He thought of his custody list running grey in the corner of his sight, faster and faster, like ash. In Mercy. A miner. A schoolteacher. A child. He did the arithmetic without wanting to, the way his mind did arithmetic, and then he stopped it, the way he had stopped the list.
Have you ever seen one come home?
“Thank you, Warden,” he said. “You’ve been very kind.”

“It’s what we’re for.” She walked with him back toward the atrium, unhurried, her hands folded. At the great doors she paused. “Since you’re here, Your Grace, may I trouble you with one of your own? It would save us sending it up.”
“One of mine.”

“The Hale case. The old man from Abundance.” She said it without any particular weight, a clerk mentioning a file. “He’s scheduled for tomorrow, the second hour. You signed his custody, so the release needs your countersign. Usually we send it to you and you sign from wherever you are. But some bishops like to attend their own. It gives the families comfort, when there are families.”
Something opened in the corner of his sight. He had not touched his temple; she had sent it. A form, plain and white, in the same font as all the others.
Release from Mercy. HALE, Stephen. Custody: Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life.
Beneath it, a blank line, waiting.
“Can it be delayed?” he said. His voice sounded quite ordinary.

Kell’s brows rose a little. “The schedule comes to us from Concord, Your Grace, and Concord’s comes from Sion. Ordinarily a bishop might petition. But this one came down already flagged.” She looked at him with mild, untroubled curiosity. “He’s refused renewal, you know. Over and over. The wardens up top say he talks to them through the glass all day long, though of course no one listens. He’s very old.” She smiled. “It will be a kindness. You’ll see.”

The fountain played in the forecourt, slow and white, each drop rising and falling as if it had all the time in the world. Sol walked past it to the car and got in and sat with his hands on the controls.

He did not sign the form. He did not close it either. All the long way up through the ice, through the violet and the deep blue and the blue, it hung in the corner of his sight, patient and white, the way it had waited for him a thousand times before, for nothing more than a thought.
